sections.b: After Jerusalem fell, Babylon's chief of the guard let Jeremiah choose where to live, and he chose to stay with the people who were left, under Gedaliah at Mizpah. After Gedaliah was murdered, the survivors asked him for God's word, rejected it, and took him and Baruch to Egypt against his will. His last words in the book are to the Judeans in Egypt, who answer him that they will keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven.

Chapter 45 turns from public history to a short word to his scribe Baruch, dated to 605 BC. Baruch is told to stop seeking great things for himself; the LORD gives him his life as loot wherever he goes.

common: Jeremiah chose to stay with the remnant at Mizpah when Babylon offered him a place at court.
uncommon: The Lives of the Prophets and Tertullian (Scorpiace 8) say Jeremiah was stoned to death by his own people in Egypt; Jeremiah itself never tells his death.

sections.h: Those who stayed and those who fled
sections.b: The exile was not one deportation. In 597, 586 and perhaps 582 Babylon took Judeans east; a poor remnant stayed under Gedaliah, and after his murder many fled to Egypt. Jeremiah 40–44 follows these last groups, who were never in Babylon, and shows that the 'exile' also included communities in Moab, Ammon, Edom and Egypt (40:11).

sections.h: Egypt as a refuge Jeremiah forbids
sections.b: After Gedaliah's murder the remnant of Judah went to Egypt for safety. Jeremiah warned that the Egypt they chose would not protect them (42:14–22), and in Tahpanhes he acted out Nebuchadnezzar's coming (43:8–13). The Law's last curse was a return to Egypt (Deuteronomy 28:68), and the first Judean colonies in the Nile valley, at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and Pathros, are the background to the later Judean garrison at Elephantine.

sections.h: Babylon's officers and rule in Judah
sections.b: Jeremiah 39 lists the Babylonian officers who sat in the Middle Gate; one name matches a Babylonian tablet of 595 BC. Babylon chose Mizpah, not Jerusalem, as its center and put Gedaliah in charge. The people who feared its revenge for his murder fled to Egypt rather than stay.

In 43:10 the LORD calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant and says he will set up his throne over the stones hidden at Tahpanhes. The Greek does not have 'my servant' here; 2QJer does. No Babylonian text says he conquered Egypt, but a fragment dated to his thirty-seventh year (568/567 BC) records a campaign.

sections.h: The remnant at Mizpah and in Egypt
sections.b: In Jeremiah 40–44 'the remnant of Judah' is a group that is addressed, chosen for building and planting if it stays (42:10) and cut off if it goes to Egypt (44:12–14). Jeremiah says that a few fugitives will return (44:14, 28). The remnant who stayed took Gedaliah's side and lost; the remnant who left took Egypt's and are told they will not last.

sections.h: The Queen of Heaven and the women's answer
sections.b: In Egypt the Judeans said they would keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, because their troubles began when they stopped. Jeremiah's answer is that the troubles came because of the incense, not for lack of it (44:15–23). The chapter is the fullest Old Testament account of ordinary family worship of a goddess, and the clearest case of two readings of the same history.

The survivors asked Jeremiah for God's word, promised to obey it, waited ten days, and then called him a liar when the answer was 'stay' (42:1–43:3). Jeremiah's last test of a prophet is the Law's: whose word comes true, God's or theirs (44:28; Deuteronomy 18:21–22).

The prophet who had been told not to pray for the people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11) is asked by the survivors to pray, and does. His answer after ten days is a promise if they stay and a warning if they go.

The sun-god's pillars at Heliopolis (Beth-shemesh in Hebrew; On in Genesis 41:45) are named in Jeremiah 43:13 as stones Nebuchadnezzar will smash. They were obelisks, tall stone shafts sacred to the sun-god Re, and not memorials of the kind the patriarchs set up.

sections.h: 'I have changed my mind about the harm I did'
sections.b: In Jeremiah 42:10 the LORD says he has changed his mind about the harm he did, using the verb nicham as in 26:3, 13, 19 and the rule of 18:7–10. The offer there is not a change of mind about justice but a promise: if the remnant stays, God builds and plants. In 45:4 the same God demolishes what he built.

sections.h: Jeremiah 44: the women of Judah in Egypt
sections.b: The women and men of Judah in Egypt say they will go on with incense, drink offerings and cakes, as they and their kings did in Judah. They believe the cult made them prosper and that stopping it brought the sword and famine. The vows are the women's, and the husbands consented (Numbers 30:6–15). Jeremiah says the LORD remembered the incense and brought the fall because of it, and he mocks their vows: let them keep them, and be cut off (44:25–27). Scholars identify the goddess with Ishtar-Astarte; the Greek calls her basilissa tou ouranou.

sections.h: The Jewish and Christian use of the title
sections.b: Radak takes the cakes of 44:19 as food prepared and served to the Queen of Heaven. Catholic teaching gives the title 'Queen' to Mary on other grounds (see the card at Jeremiah 44:17); the passage is sometimes raised in debate over that title, and Catholic teaching distinguishes the worship of a goddess, which Jeremiah condemns, from the honor given to a creature.

Gedaliah son of Ahikam, grandson of Shaphan, is the Babylonian appointee at Mizpah in 2 Kings 25:22–26 and Jeremiah 40–41. Jeremiah chooses to join him, and the commanders swear to him. He ignores a warning about Ishmael and is killed at a meal in the seventh month. A seal from Lachish names a 'Gedaliah who is over the house,' probably a pre-governor title. Jews keep the Fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri.

Baruch son of Neriah wrote Jeremiah's words down, read the scroll in the temple and is warned in a private word to stop seeking great things (Jeremiah 36; 45). In Egypt the commanders accuse him of turning Jeremiah against them (43:3), and he is taken to Egypt with him (43:6). Later books were written in his name: Baruch (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches) and 2 Baruch (in no church's canon).

Eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria came to 'the house of the LORD' with grain offerings and incense, in mourning, after the temple was burned (Jeremiah 41:5). The site stayed holy to those who had known it.

Baalis, king of the Ammonites, sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to kill Gedaliah (40:14), and Ishmael fled to Ammon after the murder (41:15). A seal from Tell el-Umeiri in Jordan names 'Milkom'ur, servant of Ba'alyasha',' probably this king.

A Cushite court official, Ebed-melech, rescued Jeremiah from the cistern (38:7–13), and the LORD promised him his life 'because you trusted in me' (39:15–18). He is the only foreigner in Jeremiah who receives a personal promise of rescue.
